title: Transfer Learning in Bandits from Unknown Adaptive Policies: Problem-Dependent Lower and Upper Bounds
abstract: Transfer learning in stochastic multi-armed bandits is typically studied assuming that prior data forms a fixed offline dataset or is generated by a known source. In practice, historical observations come from a previous adaptive decision process whose policy is unknown. We study this setting for bounded rewards in $[0,1]$. Before the online game starts, the learner receives, for each arm $k$, $N'_k$ observations drawn i.i.d.\ from an unknown distribution $ν'_k$, collected by an arbitrary and possibly data-dependent strategy, so the sample sizes $N'_k$ may be random. Source and target means satisfy $|μ_k-μ'_k|<L_k$ for known constants $(L_k)_k$. We derive an asymptotic problem-dependent lower bound and propose KL-UCB-Transfer, which combines online and historical data and achieves logarithmic regret with an improved leading constant whenever $μ'_a<μ_1-L_a$, and recovers the classical KL-UCB guarantee otherwise. Since bounding the source-target discrepancy is often unrealistic, we relax the assumption to the one-sided condition $μ_k-μ'_k<L_k$ and show that logarithmic regret can survive under misspecification, characterizing three regimes ranging from improvement to a degraded logarithmic bound to a loss of guarantee. Simulations illustrate the practical benefits of exploiting process-generated historical data.
triage_reason: bandit transfer bounds; no simulator, agent or RL-training question in any lane

title: Dexterity from Supervised Play
abstract: How can robots autonomously collect the contact-rich experience needed to learn dexterous manipulation? We present DSP: Dexterity from supervised play, a framework in which a robot learns a play policy from minutes of human play through behavior cloning, then deploys it autonomously to collect hours of interaction data to train a world model. During inference, the same play policy then guides model-predictive control (MPC) by proposing candidate action sequences for evaluation under the learned world model. To accelerate inference, we also introduce a method for distilling a closed-loop, goal-conditioned policy through self-play within the learned world model. We evaluate this framework on underactuated pushing and any-to-any in-hand pose reorientation with a multifingered hand, in simulation and real world. In real world experiment, our method outperforms hindsight behavior cloning by 69.6% in success rate and achieves comparable success to reinforcement learning with 490 times less interaction data. These results demonstrate that supervised play can autonomously collect interaction data, guide model-based planning, and enable policy learning without any task-specific demonstrations or sim-to-real transfer.
triage_reason: real-robot play data and world-model MPC; no simulator fidelity measurement

title: Whole-Body Dexterity
abstract: Current humanoid dexterous manipulation remains largely confined to end-effectors and simple grasps, falling short of humans' ability to engage the entire body by bracing and sliding bulky objects against the arms and torso. We introduce Whole-Body Dexterity (WBD), a general framework that uses the robot's body and appendages as contact surfaces to grasp and manipulate objects. Our sim-to-real pipeline first generates a dataset of feasible whole-body grasps, then trains reinforcement-learning experts on a general any-to-any repositioning objective by sampling initial and goal grasps from the dataset, and distills these experts into a single policy that uses proprioception and object geometry. We show that the distilled policy transfers zero-shot to a real Unitree G1, where it repositions a basketball and a cardboard box to regions around the torso and completes a long-horizon task that stows a box under one arm, carries it from a shelf to a table, and places it. The controller operates interactively, steered by coarse motion references from a human teleoperator. Across real-world whole-body manipulation tasks, the distilled controller completes 90% of trials, compared with 18% for direct retargeting and 4% for a generalist whole-body controller.
triage_reason: sim-to-real RL for humanoid grasps; consumer of simulators, measures nothing about them

title: When the KV Cache Is Slower Than the GPU: Scaling Remote KV Tiers for Context-Parallel Prefill
abstract: Reusing the attention KV cache across requests is a standard way to cut prefill cost in long-context LLM serving, and production systems increasingly back the per-engine cache with a remote tier shared by every engine. We study such a tier in a disaggregated deployment of GLM-5.3, an FP8 mixture-of-experts model with multi-head latent attention (MLA), on 8xB300 nodes running prefill context parallelism (PCP8). Enabling the remote tier (LMCache with a Valkey store) left median time-to-first-token unchanged but raised the 16k-token p99 from 3.96 s to 17.3 s. Replaying a production request stream on an isolated engine, we find that a remote hit took 0.88 s against 0.31 s to recompute the prompt, and that synchronous loading turned a hit-heavy stream into an unstable queue: p99 83.32 s with the GPUs 7% busy. A two-term cost model explains both: a hit pays off only if the tier delivers more than B* = sR (2.53 GB/s for this model and GPU), and a fixed per-hit engine cost (T0 ~ 0.33 s) means that hits on prompts shorter than about 17k tokens cannot beat recompute at any bandwidth. Guided by the model, we (i) shard the MLA KV store across PCP ranks, with a proof that the existing minimum-over-ranks lookup returns the longest cached prefix and a load protocol that can never desynchronize collectives; (ii) partition the remote tier by rank, one server instance per rank with no coordination, which raises GET bandwidth 6.3x to 10.76 GB/s; (iii) add asynchronous loading to the sharded store; and (iv) fix three client bugs that caused unbounded stalls. On the hit-heavy stream, with 98.5% of prompt tokens served from the remote tier, p99 falls from 83.32 s to 0.67 s. The sharded store raises prefill throughput by 14%, and by 34% together with an upstream kernel fix. All changes are submitted upstream to LMCache.
triage_reason: two-term cost model (hit pays only if tier bandwidth > sR; fixed per-hit cost) for KV reuse: a ruler for L3 cost structure

title: A Phenomenology of Neural Geometry in Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Robotic manipulation is inherently geometric, but what shape does the world take inside the policy that performs it? Prior work on vision-language-action (VLA) policies establishes that task-relevant variables are linearly readable from activations, yet readability certifies only that a variable is present and says nothing about the shape its values trace, which may be curved and multi-dimensional. Using controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes, and activation interventions, we build a taxonomy of seven task-relevant concepts in VLA models. We find that realized geometry is predominantly multi-dimensional and is shaped by the constraints under which the policy acts. Physical joint limits, for example, leave wrist orientation an open arc rather than a circle, and distance to the target, a single scalar, is realized in two orthogonal subspaces, a coarse ruler for the approach and a fine ruler for the grasp. The same geometries reappear in two further VLA models on real-world robot data, indicating that they are neither model-specific nor artifacts of simulation. We demonstrate how the findings are actionable by steering along the geometry a concept realizes. Overall, this work lays out an initial phenomenology of realized geometry in VLA policies and demonstrates that a concept's shape carries as much importance as its readability.
triage_reason: representation geometry inside VLA policies; not simulator V&V

title: Two-Stage Score Estimation for Group-Specific Diffusion Models
abstract: Generative modeling across related distributions raises a question: how can shared structure support accurate generation for a target distribution with limited observations? We develop a statistical framework for diffusion transfer that analyzes a shared pooled score together with a target-specific offset. Under Besov regularity of the pooled density and a stable hierarchical composition model for the offset, we derive convergence rates that separate the costs of learning these components and identify when a simpler offset yields a faster risk-bound rate than separate fitting. Under suitable boundary and regularity assumptions, we prove that the offset remains bounded and jointly regular as diffusion time approaches zero. These results allow the lower time cutoff to vanish polynomially and provide total-variation guarantees for diffusion models as density estimators. Synthetic simulations and image benchmarks provide a proof of concept for the framework.
triage_reason: diffusion transfer statistics; unrelated

title: The Physics Is the Network: Fast, Training-Free Neural Emulation
abstract: Neural emulation need not require learning a substitute for known physics. We investigate PolyNets that couple a continuous-time neural representation of polynomial dynamics with a simple recurrent network for discrete-time integration. When the governing coefficients are known, the resulting tensor graph requires no training and preserves the prescribed numerical scheme while enabling efficient hardware execution and parallel simulation. Using the one-dimensional Korteweg-de Vries equation, we compare PolyNet with CPU and GPU finite-difference Runge-Kutta solvers and three trained neural models: a state-map emulator, a physics-informed predictor, and a learned-tendency integrator. Analytical soliton solutions provide a reference for amplitude and phase errors across grid resolutions, 10^6 dispersively scaled time steps, ensembles of up to 10^4 trajectories, and varying initial amplitudes. PolyNet achieves accuracy comparable to the numerical solvers, including at amplitudes outside the learned models' training conditions. It combines this fidelity with high GPU throughput, approximately constant over the tested resolution range, and favorable ensemble scaling.
triage_reason: training-free PDE emulator vs RK solvers; same words (fidelity, throughput), no robot contact or RL

title: SOMA: Stack-of-Objects Manipulation using a Quadruped Robot
abstract: Executing heavy-duty physical manipulation in unpredictable environments remains a major challenge for quadrupedal robots lacking dedicated manipulators. This paper presents SOMA, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for whole-body non-prehensile manipulation of multi-object stacks using a quadruped robot. Unlike traditional methods restricted to two-dimensional planar pushing, SOMA integrates explicit robot base-height control, unlocking full three-dimensional pushing strategies. This capability enables the quadruped to manipulate complex payload stacks as a unified system while preventing relative sliding or tipping of upper layers. The architecture factorizes control into a high-level manipulation policy using a Simplified Structured State Space Sequence (S5) encoder to reason over long-horizon temporal history and predict bounded target tracking commands via Beta distributions, and a low-level locomotion policy that dynamically adapts leg stance configurations. In extensive simulation benchmarks, SOMA achieves a $90.3\%$ success rate for single-object reposing and up to $90.1\%$ for dynamic two-box stacks under stringent error margins ($0.05\text{ m}$ position error, $1^\circ$ orientation error). Finally, we validate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a Unitree Go1 quadruped robot across diverse payload masses and geometries, demonstrating active base-height adjustments to maintain traction and balance during heavy pushing tasks.
triage_reason: quadruped manipulation RL with sim-to-real; no simulator measurement

title: YUBI-Real2Sim: 3DGS Scene Verification for Reliable Policy Evaluation
abstract: Evaluating VLA policies on real robots is costly, time-consuming, and difficult to reproduce, making real-to-sim simulation essential for scalable evaluation. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables rapid real-to-sim scene generation, the reconstruction quality required for reliable policy evaluation remains unquantified. In particular, policies relying on wrist-mounted fisheye cameras (e.g., YUBI handheld gripper data) are heavily exposed to visual artifacts (holes, floaters) in wide-angle views, directly degrading task performance. To address this, we present YUBI-Real2Sim, a unified framework for 3DGS-based scene reconstruction and real-to-sim policy evaluation under dual fisheye wrist views. We develop an integrated pipeline combining 200-degree fisheye camera capture, 3DGS training, 3D foundation models for object modeling, and MuJoCo-based physical simulation, reproducing the observed real-world policy ordering in eight of nine scene-task comparisons. Using this framework, we construct a benchmark across two bimanual robot platforms, three scenes, three tasks, and dual pi0.5-based policies. This systematically measures real-to-sim rank agreement and evaluates policy sensitivity against counterfactual 3DGS artifacts (ceiling holes, floaters, warping) and capture disturbances. We further analyze whether novel-view quality scores can indicate policy-ranking reliability under a scene-held-out evaluation protocol. The results show task-dependent performance and limitations of quality-based reliability prediction, highlighting the need to assess reconstruction quality when using Real2Sim for policy evaluation. These results do not yet establish a generally reliable scene-acceptance rule. Project Page: https://yubi-real2sim.airoa.io.
triage_reason: real-to-sim rank agreement and policy sensitivity to injected scene artifacts: simulator fidelity as measurement validity (visual, MuJoCo)

title: Federated Unlearning of Quantum Data via Classical Shadows
abstract: Quantum federated learning trains a quantum neural network (QNN) across nodes that hold quantum data, such as the states of quantum sensors. To forget data, unlearning methods for quantum models replay them, and federated unlearning from stored updates removes whole nodes only. Quantum data cannot be replayed, since a state is consumed when measured and cannot be cloned. We propose Shadow-based Data Erasure (SHADE), in which each node records a classical shadow of every training state, a few randomized single-qubit measurements taken at training time. The gradient and curvature of a QNN on a state are expectations of observables, so SHADE estimates them for the forget data from the shadows at any later parameters and removes their effect by a federated Newton correction. Only classical estimates cross the network. We prove that the shadow size needed for a target unlearning error grows exponentially in the size of the backward light cone of the measured observable and not in the number of qubits. In simulation with 50 nodes and on edge boards, SHADE matches the forget accuracy of retraining within 0.5 points, without replay and in under 0.2 s.
triage_reason: quantum federated unlearning; unrelated

title: LunaTP: Enabling Efficient and Scalable Tensor Product for Equivariant MLIPs
abstract: Equivariant machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) promise atomistic simulations with accuracy approaching that of quantum-mechanical calculations. However, the high computational cost of their core Clebsch--Gordan tensor product (CGTP) convolutions severely limits model scalability and efficiency. In this paper, we rethink the parallel execution of CGTP convolutions and introduce LunaTP. Built on node-centric execution, LunaTP exploits path-group parallelism and multi-level reuse to accelerate CGTP convolutions and higher-order derivative computation while preserving the underlying mathematical formulation. On an NVIDIA H100 GPU, LunaTP achieves kernel speedups of up to 250.0$\times$ over e3nn and 17.1$\times$ over OpenEquivariance. It also delivers end-to-end training throughput gains of up to 28.7$\times$ over e3nn and 3.11$\times$ over OpenEquivariance. Finally, LunaTP demonstrates scalability and robust performance across models, workload scales, and GPUs, delivering substantial acceleration for training and atomistic simulation with high-accuracy equivariant MLIPs.
triage_reason: kernel for equivariant interatomic potentials; kernel-level, no agent or RL workload (L3 out of scope)

title: Back to the Future: Reverse-Consequence Modeling for Long-Horizon Particle Dynamics
abstract: Accurate prediction of object trajectories is fundamental to mechanical understanding and robotic control. However, autoregressive models inherently suffer from cumulative errors, leading to severe drift in long-horizon rollouts. Observing that in many physical systems with dissipative or convergence-to-rest behavior, the final states are often more predictable than transient dynamics (e.g., a sliding object resting under friction or a pendulum stabilizing at equilibrium), we propose ReStep, a cascaded approach that reverses the conventional forward-prediction paradigm. ReStep first employs a stochastic model to directly predict the final state, then leverages Anchored Diffusion to generate goal-conditioned intermediate trajectories. By conditioning on both ''boundary states'', it effectively constrains dynamics and reduces uncertainty, producing physically plausible and temporally coherent transitions. We further integrate ReStep dynamics as the physical engine within a 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline, enabling a unified physical-visual framework for intuitive inference from images. Extensive experiments on diverse rigid and non-rigid collision datasets show that ReStep achieves superior long-term accuracy, substantially mitigating error accumulation via reverse-consequence modeling.
triage_reason: learned reverse-consequence dynamics model; builds a model, L5 measures engines

title: Space-Time Parallel Direct Numerical Simulation of Rayleigh-Bénard Convection
abstract: Rayleigh-Bénard convection (RBC) is a model for turbulent flow and challenging to simulate by direct numerical simulation (DNS). Adequate resolution of all relevant length scales requires very fine grids in space and stability restrictions can dictate small step sizes. In this paper, we investigate the use of parallel spectral deferred correction (SDC) as a high-order time-stepping method to reduce wall-clock times of direct numerical simulation of RBC. Performance results on JUSUF (CPUs) and JUPITER (GPUs) with two different codes show parallel SDC can offer some concurrency along the temporal axis plus larger maximum stable time steps. Taken together, this allows for a reduction of wall-clock time required for simulations over one free-fall time by having to compute fewer steps and being able to mitigate the higher cost per time step through temporal parallelization.
triage_reason: parallel-in-time DNS of convection; numerics without robot learning

title: Quota-Based Aging for Prediction-Guided Scheduling in LLM Serving
abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving systems use token-level continuous batching to improve resource utilization, but heterogeneous response lengths complicate request scheduling. Prediction-guided short-first scheduling reduces average latency but can severely delay long requests, while unrestricted aging may over-promote delayed long requests under congestion. We propose Quota-Based Aging (QBA), a lightweight policy that combines predicted short-first admission with quota-bounded, debt-enforced promotion of aged predicted-long requests. We also use a reduced M/G/n queueing surrogate, calibrated from simulator traces, to explain first-order mean-latency trends. QBA is evaluated using a serving-aware event-driven simulator that models decode-priority batching, chunked prefill, token-budget constraints, and KV-cache-safe admission. We compare QBA with FCFS, predicted short-first, and aggressive aging under asymmetric prediction errors on synthetic and production-derived workloads. The evaluation considers queueing delay, throughput, utilization, and class-conditional tail performance. Results show that QBA provides a controllable middle ground between aggressive short-first prioritization and unrestricted aging, substantially reducing long-request tail latency while retaining much of the mean-latency benefit of prediction-guided scheduling.
triage_reason: LLM serving admission policy; no agent or RL workload attached

title: RadixFlow: Filling Execution Bubbles in Prefix-Cached Hybrid LLM Serving
abstract: Prefix reuse improves LLM inference by sharing the KV cache of common prompt prefixes. This helps only if the scheduler can execute a matched branch in the current worker round. Schedulers assume that a matched prefix is ready, which holds for full attention but fails for hybrid LLMs. There, a branch (the consumer) may need recurrent state that another branch (the producer) is still computing in the same round. The native scheduler stops its waiting-queue scan at this blocked consumer, and the resulting head-of-line blocking creates \emph{execution bubbles}: idle batch slots that independent work could fill. We introduce RadixFlow, which decouples prefix matching from state readiness. Its state-ready traversal turns a global scan barrier into a local wait: only the consumer is blocked until the next round, while feasible independent branches keep filling the batch under the native state check. On five hybrid models, RadixFlow lowers mean latency by 3\% to 24\% and worker rounds by 11\% to 44\% at almost unchanged reuse. On the larger Qwen3.5 models, ablations show that most of the gain comes from traversal, which adds little on a full-attention control. Heavier rounds limit how much of this saving reaches latency.
triage_reason: prefix-cache scheduler fix for hybrid models; serving only, no agent or RL workload

title: Stable Token-level Scheduling for Serverless LLM Inference
abstract: Serverless inference is emerging as an efficient deployment model for Large Language Models (LLMs) due to its ability to elastically scale resources, improve GPU utilization through resource sharing, and reduce infrastructure costs. However, existing approaches primarily optimize time to first token (TTFT) while overlooking inter-token latency (ITL), a key determinant of user experience during response generation. We observe that LLM inference comprises a computation-intensive prefill stage and a bandwidth-bound decode stage, where admitting new requests can disrupt ongoing decoding and increase latency. To address this, we propose Token Window Pacing (TWP), a closed-loop scheduling framework that leverages runtime feedback from ITL, queue depth, and workload characteristics to regulate request admission at the token level instead of the batch level. TWP dynamically adjusts a selfregulating token window and incorporates chunk-based prefill to minimize interference from incoming requests. Experiments on realistic serverless workloads show that TWP delivers stable TTFT, significantly reduces latency spikes, lowers P99 tail latency, minimizes ITL variation, and improves throughput by up to 45% over ServerlessLLM and 58% over conventional schedulers. These results demonstrate that feedback-driven tokenlevel scheduling enables stable, high-throughput serverless LLM inference without modifying the underlying model.
triage_reason: serverless inference token pacing; no agent or RL workload

title: Formal-Verification-Guided Bayesian Optimization for Non-Intrusive Last-Mile Coverage Closure
abstract: Last-mile functional coverage closure for modern chip designs remains costly because a mature UVM environment exposes many controls while direct hits on the remaining bins are sparse. We present a non-intrusive workflow that closes pre-defined bins in an existing, human-authored functional coverage model; it does not synthesize verification objectives from the design specification. The workflow first uses abstract-syntax-tree (AST) parsing and cone-of-influence (COI) tracing to map each residual target to existing testbench knobs. Under a matched 20-simulation budget, Bayesian optimization (BO) is compared with continued constrained-random verification (CRV) and random search over the same AST/COI-reduced space. Formal reachability then removes only targets supported by complete unreachability proofs, after which retained targets are grouped by formal difficulty and processed by group-specific BO under a second matched 20-simulation budget. Cleanup and grouping never add numerator bins; only simulator coverage artifacts do. On OpenTitan AES, first-pass reduced-space BO reaches 241/271 bins; formal cleanup removes two denominator bins; the integrated post-cleanup stage - difficulty grouping, policy routing, and group-specific BO - adds 20 simulator-confirmed hits, yielding 261/271 raw coverage (96.31%) and 261/269 effective coverage (97.03%). On Entropy Source, first-pass reduced-space BO reaches 2117/2277 bins; formal cleanup removes ten denominator bins; the integrated post-cleanup stage - difficulty grouping, policy routing, and group-specific BO - adds 93 simulator-confirmed hits, yielding 2210/2277 raw coverage (97.06%) and 2210/2267 effective coverage (97.49%). These results characterize the integrated diagnosis-and-search workflow; the present evaluation does not isolate the causal contributions of difficulty classification, policy routing, and post-cleanup BO.
triage_reason: chip verification coverage closure; unrelated

title: Trust-Calibrated VLA Policy Post-Training with Evolving Imagination
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are often pretrained via imitation learning, making reinforcement learning (RL) post-training important when deployment moves beyond demonstration coverage. Existing refinement paradigms expose a reliability--efficiency tension: model-free refinement avoids simulator bias but is interaction-intensive, whereas model-based refinement can exploit unreliable imagination even as its simulator adapts. We propose Model-Evolving Reinforcement Learning (MERL), a trust-calibrated framework that couples policy optimization with an online-updated simulator comprising a world model and a reward proxy head. Across stages, simulator reliability controls the imagined-data ratio and rollout horizon; within rollouts, chunk-level trust controls replay selection and optimization weight. For recursive imagination without exact grounded continuations, a residual predictor estimates trust without querying future ground truth. On perturbed LIBERO-PRO tasks, MERL reaches 79.7% average success, improves high-threshold learning speed by 10.9% over the matched model-free control, and outperforms same-protocol external baselines across three training seeds. Fixed-data adaptation from 50 demonstrations per task achieves 80.0% average success on two physical-robot tasks.
triage_reason: neighbor: policy exploiting an unreliable learned simulator, with per-chunk trust gating imagined data; the exploit-share idea in a world-model setting

title: Compute-optimal data scaling for neural surrogates via multi-fidelity training
abstract: Neural surrogates for Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) are usually trained on synthetic data from numerical simulators. As models grow and scaling laws demand larger datasets, the cost of data generation often outweighs the training cost and becomes the bottleneck in the scaling quest. Unlike data in other domains, however, each PDE sample has a tunable cost that depends on its numerical fidelity, with the resulting cost-accuracy trade-off governed by known convergence rates. We exploit this property by formalizing neural surrogate training as a function of both data quantity and fidelity under a fixed data generation compute budget, treating fidelity as a fine-grained discrete spectrum rather than a binary distinction. Building on this, we show that multi-fidelity training enables Pareto-optimal error scaling against data generation compute. By using simulations at lower fidelities as an additional training signal, training on the optimal fidelity mixture matches the accuracy of high-fidelity-only training, with up to $6.3\times$ less data generation compute across our settings. We validate these findings across six PDE problems spanning structured grids and unstructured meshes, two distinct error sources (discretization and iterative-solver error), and four surrogate architectures, totaling over 7,000 training runs.
triage_reason: fidelity as a tunable dose with known convergence rates; compute-matched fidelity mixtures; two error sources (time step, iterative solver) = L5's knobs

title: MCCL: Measurement-based Collective Communication Library
abstract: Collective communication is a critical performance bottleneck in large-scale distributed training. Existing libraries and synthesis frameworks compute open-loop schedules once, assuming a static topology and peak link capacities. In production, however, persistent gray failures can silently degrade link throughput and latency for hours, causing pre-computed schedules to lose much of their efficiency during execution. In this paper, we present Measurement-based Collective Communication Library (MCCL), a collective communication library that closes the loop between runtime network measurement and dynamic schedule synthesis. MCCL passively measures GPU-to-GPU throughput, detects persistent degradation, re-synthesizes the affected communication-intensive schedules with warm-started synthesizers, and hot-swaps them without interrupting training. We validate the complete loop on a multi-node hardware prototype and use simulations to evaluate cluster-scale scenarios. In our experiments, MCCL incurs negligible overhead (<2%) while maintaining high measurement accuracy (<1.2% error) and low schedule hot-swap time (about 12 ms). Notably, under gray failures, MCCL reduces training time by up to 4.99x over static schedules on simulated training workloads for state-of-the-art LLMs such as Llama and DeepSeek.
triage_reason: collective communication re-synthesis; training infra without agent or RL workload

title: Is the Platform Part of the Measurement? A Protocol and Simulation Study for Cross-Platform Equivalence of Machine-Labelled Policy Sentiment
abstract: Comparing machine-labelled sentiment across social media platforms is now routine: differences in classifier scores between platforms are read as differences in public opinion. These comparisons rest on an assumption that the classifier measures the same construct, on the same scale, on every platform. Some studies check a classifier's validity platform by platform, but to our knowledge none has modelled the platform as a facet of the classifier's measurement. We adapt the psychometric equivalence toolkit (generalizability theory, measurement invariance and differential item functioning, and score linking) to machine-labelled policy sentiment, treating the platform as a survey mode, and specify a six-step protocol with anchor events fixed in advance, an anchor-density audit, and a two-classifier convergence control. A simulation with known ground truth illustrates what the assumption can cost in one generating configuration fixed in advance: across 500 replications, because the platforms measure through different functions, a pooled index that takes platform scores at face value reports the wrong sign of aggregate sentiment on nearly a quarter of days, whereas an index adjusted with each platform's known measurement function does so on under one day in sixty on average. A case study of the instrument from the first author's MSc dissertation, a fine-tuned BERT classifier over 255,446 UK economic-policy comments from Twitter/X, Reddit, YouTube, and Quora, motivates the design and illustrates the instrument-dependence the protocol addresses. The full four-platform application, under fresh collection with the pre-specified design, is the designated follow-up study. The protocol lets a researcher test whether pooling platforms is defensible in a given corpus, or whether platform scores must be linked before any average is taken.
triage_reason: protocol treating the measurement context as a facet (G-theory, DIF, score linking) for an ML classifier; template for harness/simulator-as-facet in L1

title: Explaining Heterogeneous Treatment Effects with Causal Forests and the Hoeffding Functional Decomposition
abstract: The estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects is a central objective of causal inference. However, state-of-the-art algorithms to solve this task are based on machine learning principles, and thus behave as black boxes. Consequently, the identification of covariates driving heterogeneity remains a challenging and open problem. To address this limitation, we introduce CausalTreeHFD, an interpretable extension of causal forests, based on the Hoeffding functional decomposition adapted to tree ensembles. Our approach decomposes predictions of conditional average treatment effects (CATE) into contributions from individual covariates and pairwise interactions, providing a direct characterization of the factors driving treatment effect heterogeneity. We establish the consistency of CausalTreeHFD, which converges towards the Hoeffding decomposition of the underlying CATE function, under standard assumptions for the analysis of causal forests. Experiments on simulated and real datasets show that CausalTreeHFD accurately identifies relevant covariates and interactions, and precisely recovers their contributions to heterogeneous treatment effects.
triage_reason: causal forest decomposition; unrelated

title: Distributional Regression for Arbitrary Response Variables Using ReLU Neural Networks
abstract: This paper develops a unified framework for distributional regression with arbitrary response variables. Rather than relying on scalar thresholds or Euclidean structure, we model conditional event probabilities indexed by measurable sets, which extends distributional regression to general response spaces while retaining a direct connection to classical event-based formulations. Within this framework, we study two complementary estimators: a preliminary estimator based on separate regression of event indicators, and a constrained estimator that enforces inclusion-consistent predictions through a directed acyclic graph (DAG) over a finite set family. We establish general error bounds for both estimators and further specialize the results to dense ReLU networks, yielding explicit convergence rates overcoming the curse of dimensionality. Simulation studies and real-data experiments further demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the proposed framework.
triage_reason: distributional regression theory; unrelated

title: MSC: Multi-Stage Caster-aware Control Framework with Uncertainty-Aware NMPC and RL-based Execution Layer
abstract: Freely swiveling casters are widely adopted in industrial AMRs/SDVs for their mechanical simplicity and load capacity. However, caster misalignment during low-speed or high-curvature maneuvers induces strong contact nonlinearities, widening the planning-execution gap between commanded $(v, ω)$ and realized motion. Existing caster-aware strategies are highly sensitive to state-estimation reliability, causing unstable execution in uncertain transition regimes. To address this, we present Multi-Stage Caster-aware Control (MSC), a planning-execution integrated hierarchical framework featuring two core mechanisms. First, an uncertainty-aware NMPC (CU-MPC) dynamically schedules caster-aware costs and input regularization using predictive uncertainty to suppress overly aggressive maneuvers. Second, a reinforcement learning-based execution layer estimates and predicts caster states under partial observability, transforming high-level velocity commands into physically executable wheel speeds adapted to current contact conditions. Validations in Isaac Sim and real robots demonstrate that MSC offers a clear comparative advantage over existing decoupled compensation approaches by significantly improving caster-state estimation accuracy, minimizing misalignment, and enhancing tracking robustness in caster-sensitive maneuvers.
triage_reason: caster-aware control validated in Isaac Sim; consumer, no fidelity measurement

title: Queue-Aware Token Communications: Bridging AI Representation and Wireless Service
abstract: The rapid advancement of foundation models and edge intelligence is transforming wireless networks from data-oriented communication systems into artificial intelligence (AI)-native service platforms. Token communications (TokenCom) has emerged as a promising paradigm that directly transmits task-oriented AI representations. However, existing studies typically assume that generated tokens can be transmitted immediately, overlooking the queueing dynamics arising from the mismatch between token workload generation and time-varying wireless service capability. To address this limitation, we introduce Queue-Aware TokenCom, which explicitly incorporates token queues into the AI service pipeline. We present an end-to-end architecture integrating AI representation generation, token workload management, wireless transmission, and downstream task inference. We then discuss two key design directions: budget-aware token representation optimization and queue-aware token service optimization, with the token budget serving as a critical interface between AI performance and communication efficiency. Moreover, we investigate fixed and adaptive token budget strategies to characterize the fundamental tradeoff between AI performance and communication efficiency in dynamic wireless environments. Finally, we outline research directions toward closed-loop, task-aware, and scalable TokenCom systems.
triage_reason: wireless token queueing; unrelated to agent systems

title: Audit residuals as Kalman innovations: whiteness, NIS and solver-knob signatures
abstract: In control theory, 'is the model or simulator wrong' is solved by treating the prediction error as an innovation: divide it by its predicted spread, test the sequence for bias, whiteness and chi-square covariance, let observability decide which errors can be seen from the logged measurements, and project the residual on each fault's signature direction to say which component failed; carried into L5, that says the per-step audit d_t = ||F_ref(x_t,u_t) - x_{t+1}|| should be an innovation, not a distance: whiten it by the reference set's own step spread S_t (across finer time steps, more solver iterations, other contact models and GPU-batch seeds), test the whole rollout for bias, lag autocorrelation and NIS exceedance instead of counting steps above a fixed kappa, project it on the signature directions of the engine knobs (iteration cap -> constraint-force and penetration direction; time step -> impact-velocity direction; contact softening -> restitution direction) so the audit names the knob a policy exploits, and log contact forces and penetration because iteration-cap errors sit in the near-unobservable subspace of a position-only log until they compound.

sentences: A Kalman filter (a recursive estimator that predicts the next measurement from a model, then corrects on what arrives) produces an innovation at every step, the gap between the arriving measurement and the model's prediction; when the model is right, the innovation divided by its predicted spread is zero-mean, white (uncorrelated from step to step) and has identity covariance, so the question 'is my model wrong' is answered by testing the innovation sequence for a bias, a color (autocorrelation) or a covariance change, the last by the normalized innovation squared (NIS, the innovation squared over its predicted variance), which is chi-square with as many degrees of freedom as the measurement has dimensions.

The tests trade detection delay against false alarms through a sliding window and a threshold at a chosen significance level; a scalar summary such as the trace misses faults that the full covariance shows, and the covariance test detected an F-16 gyro fault 14 steps after onset where the sum statistic took 65.

A model error is detectable only if its effect reaches the measurements (Chow 1976: a failure 'is not detectable if it cannot be observed by the system's sensors'; the undetectable directions are the unobservable subspace over the window), and each fault type has a signature direction in innovation space, so a likelihood-ratio search over fault size and onset time attributes the error to a source instead of only flagging it.
sources: https://skoge.folk.ntnu.no/prost/proceedings/ifac2008/data/papers/0071.pdf — Hajiyev, 'Testing the Covariance Matrix of the Innovation Sequence in Application to Aircraft Sensor Fault Detection', IFAC World Congress 2008 (cites Mehra & Peschon 1971 for the white, zero-mean, identity-covariance property of the normalized innovation)

https://dspace.mit.edu/bitstream/1721.1/1257/1/R-0645-18318738.pdf — Chow, 'Analytical Studies of the Generalized Likelihood Ratio Technique for Failure Detection', MIT ESL-R-645, 1976 (detectability = observability; failure signatures as directions in residual space)

https://arxiv.org/pdf/1807.08855 — Chen, Heckman, Julier, Ahmed, 'Weak in the NEES?: Auto-tuning Kalman Filters with Bayesian Optimization' (NIS definition, chi-square with n_z degrees of freedom, online use without ground truth)

import_sentence: In control theory, 'is the model or simulator wrong' is solved by treating the prediction error as an innovation: divide it by its predicted spread, test the sequence for bias, whiteness and chi-square covariance, let observability decide which errors can be seen from the logged measurements, and project the residual on each fault's signature direction to say which component failed; carried into L5, that says the per-step audit d_t = ||F_ref(x_t,u_t) - x_{t+1}|| should be an innovation, not a distance: whiten it by the reference set's own step spread S_t (across finer time steps, more solver iterations, other contact models and GPU-batch seeds), test the whole rollout for bias, lag autocorrelation and NIS exceedance instead of counting steps above a fixed kappa, project it on the signature directions of the engine knobs (iteration cap -> constraint-force and penetration direction; time step -> impact-velocity direction; contact softening -> restitution direction) so the audit names the knob a policy exploits, and log contact forces and penetration because iteration-cap errors sit in the near-unobservable subspace of a position-only log until they compound.

predicts.statement: On coarse-trained (iteration-capped) policies re-simulated under a converged reference, the whitened innovation sequence e_t = S_t^{-1/2}(x_{t+1} - F_ref(x_t,u_t)) fails the whiteness test (Ljung-Box on lags 1-5 at alpha = 0.05) and the per-episode NIS exceeds its chi-square 95% bound on a majority of exploit episodes, while the per-step count of d_t > kappa flags fewer of the same episodes at the same false-alarm rate on fine-trained policies.
predicts.expected: At matched false-alarm rate, whiteness or NIS reaches AUROC at least 0.05 above the kappa count for separating coarse-trained from fine-trained policies on two contact-rich tasks, because exploits that live as small persistent penetration below kappa show up as color (autocorrelation) and bias, not as large single steps (judgment: 55 percent).
predicts.field_assumes: The lane and its nearest incumbents assume a per-step distance threshold suffices: SAPU drops episodes with over 1 mm interpenetration, GAUGE reports generalized trajectory error, the L5 instrument thresholds d_t at a calibrated kappa.
predicts.would_change: If the sequence tests flag no more than the threshold does (AUROC gain below 0.05 on both tasks), the import is a rename and the ruler stays d_t > kappa; if they flag exploits the threshold misses, rho (share of return on suspicious steps) is redefined on the sequence statistic, SAPU-style per-episode filters are shown to under-count, and position-only audits are shown to be blind to iteration-cap errors.

identifiability: The innovation is random given (x_t, u_t, the engine's solver setting, the GPU-batch seed); F_ref at one setting is deterministic, so the spread S_t comes from the declared reference set (finer dt, more iterations, alternative contact model, batch seeds) and from nothing else; the policy's temperature does not enter because x_t, u_t are conditioned on. The statistic is a property of the (engine setting, visited-state distribution) pair and depends on the protocol through the declared reference set, which the record must name. Observability clause: errors from a capped Newton or conjugate-gradient solver appear first in constraint forces and penetration depth and reach joint positions only through the velocity jump at contact, so from a position-only log they lie near the unobservable subspace over a short window; the audit log must carry contact forces, penetration and post-impact velocities for the test to have power.

probe.design: MuJoCo Warp / MJX on two contact-rich MuJoCo Playground tasks (one toss/catch or in-hand reorientation, one landing), solver iteration caps {1, 5, 50}, PPO with 3 seeds per setting (18 policies); roll out 100 episodes per policy; re-simulate every visited (x_t,u_t) under a reference set of 6 settings (converged iterations, dt/4, dt/8, two other contact models, 3 batch seeds) to get F_ref and S_t; compute whitened e_t, per-episode NIS, Ljung-Box whiteness on lags 1-5, mean bias, and the projection of e_t on three knob-signature directions estimated from single-knob perturbations; compare ROC of (a) count of d_t > kappa, (b) NIS, (c) whiteness, (d) signature projection, against the label coarse-trained vs fine-trained and against the performance drop when each policy is evaluated under the converged engine.
probe.cost: About 60 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (training 18 small policies at about 2 GPU-hours each, re-simulation and statistics under 25 GPU-hours), 5 working days, no dollars beyond compute.
probe.kills_if: AUROC(whiteness) - AUROC(kappa count) < 0.05 and AUROC(NIS) - AUROC(kappa count) < 0.05 on both tasks, or |Spearman| between the sequence statistics and the performance drop under the converged engine is below 0.3 on both tasks; either result means the innovation view adds nothing beyond the fixed threshold and the import is filed as no-import with the ROC table as the footnote.

title: Gauge R&R for GPU physics engines: can the simulator resolve the policies it ranks?
abstract: In reliability engineering and metrology, 'is the test stimulus itself a trustworthy model' is solved by treating the instrument as a gauge and running a gauge R&R study — repeatability, reproducibility and bias measured on fixed reference items and compared, as %GRR and ndc, to the differences the gauge is used to resolve — before any reading is trusted; carried into L5, that says a GPU-batched physics engine is a gauge whose 'parts' are frozen policies, whose reading is episode return (or per-step state), and whose repeatability (same world, seed, batch slot, repeated), reproducibility (across batch position, batch size, GPU, engine) and bias (against a converged reference step) must be reported as a %GRR against the policy-to-policy return differences people read off it, with ndc telling how many distinguishable policy levels the engine can actually resolve.

sentences: In metrology a measuring instrument (a 'gauge') is characterized before it is trusted by a nested study on a fixed reference item: repeatability is the spread of J back-to-back readings under identical conditions (NIST level 1, pooled s_1 = sqrt(sum s_1lk^2 / LK)), reproducibility is the spread of condition-averages when something is deliberately changed (day, operator, instrument; NIST levels 2 and 3, s_2 and s_3), and the uncertainty of one reading is their combination s_R = sqrt(s_runs^2 + s_days^2 + s_1^2) with s_days = sqrt(s_2^2 - s_1^2/J) and s_runs = sqrt(s_3^2 - s_2^2/K).

Bias is the offset of the gauge's mean reading from a reference of known value and is examined separately from spread, under the headings resolution, linearity, hysteresis, drift and differences among gauges and configurations.

A gauge is accepted only relative to what it must discriminate: AIAG MSA combines repeatability ('equipment variation', EV) and reproducibility ('appraiser variation', AV, appraiser = operator) into GRR, compares it to the variation of the items being measured ('part variation', PV) via %GRR, calls under 10% acceptable, 10-30% marginal and over 30% unacceptable, and requires the number of distinct categories ndc = 1.41 * PV / GRR to be at least 5; the GUM frames the same thing as an uncertainty budget where every component (Type A from repeated observations, Type B from other knowledge) is listed and combined into one standard uncertainty.
sources: https://itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/mpc/section4/mpc44.htm — NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 2.4.4 'How do we quantify variability of measurements?' (nested design, s_1/s_2/s_3, s_R formula; fetched)

https://help.sigmazone.com/quantum-xl/v17/statistical-tools/msa/msa-statistics — MSA statistics page citing AIAG MSA Reference Manual 3rd ed. p.77 (%GRR thresholds 10/30) and p.117 (ndc = 1.41*PV/GRR, ndc >= 5) (fetched; the AIAG manual itself is paywalled)
https://doi.org/10.59161/JCGM100-2008E — JCGM 100:2008, Evaluation of measurement data — Guide to the expression of uncertainty in measurement (GUM) (landing page fetched; abstract only)

import_sentence: In reliability engineering and metrology, 'is the test stimulus itself a trustworthy model' is solved by treating the instrument as a gauge and running a gauge R&R study — repeatability, reproducibility and bias measured on fixed reference items and compared, as %GRR and ndc, to the differences the gauge is used to resolve — before any reading is trusted; carried into L5, that says a GPU-batched physics engine is a gauge whose 'parts' are frozen policies, whose reading is episode return (or per-step state), and whose repeatability (same world, seed, batch slot, repeated), reproducibility (across batch position, batch size, GPU, engine) and bias (against a converged reference step) must be reported as a %GRR against the policy-to-policy return differences people read off it, with ndc telling how many distinguishable policy levels the engine can actually resolve.

predicts.statement: For deterministic frozen policies on contact-rich GPU-simulated tasks (e.g., in-hand cube rotation, quadruped on rough terrain in Isaac Lab / MJX / Genesis), the engine-only gauge variance of episode return — repeatability plus reproducibility across batch size and batch position, with the policy and initial state held fixed — gives %GRR above 30% against the return gaps (3-10%) that papers report as method improvements, and ndc below 5; on smooth tasks (e.g., cartpole, flat-ground locomotion) %GRR is below 10%.
predicts.expected: Judgment, not evidence: probability 0.6 that at least one of three contact-rich tasks shows %GRR > 30% at batch sizes >= 4096 with default iteration caps, and that the engine-gauge component accounts for 20-50% of what papers call 'seed variance' (the std over training seeds); bias against a converged reference (finer dt, more solver iterations) exceeds the repeatability band on the contact-rich tasks, i.e., the engine is precise but inaccurate where it is precise and both imprecise and inaccurate where contact dominates.
predicts.field_assumes: Robot-RL practice treats the simulator as a noiseless oracle: variance is reported over training seeds and attributed to learning; GPUSimBench documents run-to-run and inter-environment variability as a reproducibility concern, not as a measurement-resolution limit, and no engine ships a repeatability/reproducibility/bias specification or a minimum resolvable return difference.
predicts.would_change: If %GRR of the engine alone exceeds 30% against reported method gaps on any widely used task, then a share of published 'A beats B by 5%' results on that task are gauge noise and every leaderboard built on that engine needs a resolution floor (ndc) column; if instead %GRR < 10% everywhere and bias sits inside the repeatability band, the belief 'GPU non-determinism matters for conclusions' is killed with a number and the lane's audit can drop the batch-slot axis.

identifiability: Random given: fixed engine build, fixed GPU model, fixed batch size and batch slot, fixed seed, fixed initial state, fixed policy run with deterministic actions (argmax / mean action; temperature 0 so the policy contributes zero decision variance by construction). What remains in the repeatability term is only the engine's floating-point reduction order under GPU thread scheduling — a property of the engine+hardware system, not of the protocol. Reproducibility factors (batch position, batch size, GPU model, engine) are chosen and crossed by the experimenter, so the reproducibility term is a property of the engine family under the stated factor ranges and must be reported with those ranges. Bias is defined against a named reference step (CPU double precision, dt/4, uncapped Newton iterations) and is a property of the engine configuration, not of the policy. title: pass^k is one point on a survival curve; report the hazard over steps
abstract: In reliability engineering, 'how reliable is this unit' is answered by estimating the survival function and the hazard rate over operating time from failure-time data with censoring, and reading the failure mechanism off the hazard's shape (falling = born broken, flat = memoryless, rising = wear-out); carried into L1, that says an agent's pass^k on a task is the k-th power of one point of a survival curve over steps, R(T)^k at the step budget T, and that the field should report R(t) and the hazard h(t) over turns or tool calls with budget-exhausted runs marked censored, because two agents or two model versions with equal pass^k can have opposite hazard shapes (fail-at-the-fork early vs degrade late), which pass^k cannot distinguish and which call for different fixes.

sentences: Reliability is not a number but a curve: the survival function R(t) is the probability a unit is still working at time t, and the quantity that characterizes it is the hazard h(t) = f(t)/R(t), which NIST defines as 'the (instantaneous) rate of failure for the survivors' at t; the two are tied by H(t) = -ln R(t), so the whole hazard curve, not one reliability figure, is the object the field estimates.

The shape of the hazard over life names the failure mechanism: the 'bathtub' has an early period 'characterized by a high but rapidly decreasing failure rate' (infant mortality, units that were broken from the start), a long flat middle where 'the failure rate levels off and remains roughly constant', and a late rise 'as materials wear out'; the Weibull model indexes all three with one shape number gamma through h(t) = (gamma/alpha)(t/alpha)^(gamma-1) (falling for gamma<1, constant for gamma=1 where it 'reduces to the Exponential Model', rising for gamma>1).

Units still running when the test stops are censored, not failed ('When not all units on test fail we have censored data'): Type I when the test stops at a fixed time, interval ('readout') when only a window containing the failure is known, and every unit yields 'exactly one of' a run-time without failure, an exact failure time, or an interval; separately, a measuring instrument (gauge) is trusted only after a gauge R&R study quantifies its repeatability (short-term, same conditions), reproducibility (day-to-day) and stability (run-to-run) variability.

predicts.statement: On tau-bench retail tasks whose pass^1 lies in [0.25, 0.75] (the 'coin-flip' tasks) with k=8 runs per task and an open-weight agent, the step of first unrecoverable error (located by a judge, audited by counterfactual forking on a subset) has a non-constant hazard: a discrete-time Weibull fit gives a shape gamma whose 95% interval excludes 1 in at least 50% of these tasks, and the sign of gamma-1 splits the coin-flip tasks into two clusters (early-fork, gamma<1; wear-out, gamma>1) that are indistinguishable by pass^1 or pass^8. Second clause: runs that end by hitting the turn or token budget make up at least 10% of recorded failures for at least one model, and scoring them as censored instead of failed moves pass^8 by at least 3 points.
predicts.expected: Judgment: both clusters exist and the early-fork cluster is the majority (roughly 60/40), because tau-bench failures concentrate at one or two policy-interpretation turns near the start of the conversation, with a wear-out minority driven by self-conditioning on earlier errors (the mechanism 2509.09677 reports: 'models become more likely to make mistakes when the context contains their errors from prior turns').
predicts.field_assumes: The lane treats a task as a Bernoulli coin with one success probability p and reports pass^k = p^k (tau-bench 2406.12045 proposes pass^k 'to evaluate the reliability of agent behavior over multiple trials'); where a time axis is used at all, a constant per-step hazard is assumed (Ord 2505.05115: 'a constant rate of failing during each minute a human would take to do the task'; 2509.09677 compounds a per-step accuracy), and budget-exhausted runs are counted as failures, never as censored.
predicts.would_change: If the shape clusters exist, a leaderboard column changes: pass^k is supplemented by (R(t) curve, gamma, censored share) per task family, and 'version A is more reliable than version B' becomes a statement about which part of the curve moved. If instead gamma=1 holds almost everywhere, that is the citable negative: the constant-hazard model that Ord fit across tasks also holds within runs, pass^k is a sufficient statistic for agent reliability, and the lane's point-estimate habit is vindicated for the first time with evidence rather than convention.

identifiability: Random given the task, the agent's sampling temperature, the user simulator's temperature and the tool environment's stochasticity; a temperature-0 agent on a deterministic environment with a fixed-seed simulator has a step-function survival curve and no hazard to estimate, so the hazard is a property of the agent-plus-protocol system at the stated temperatures, not of the agent alone (tau-bench's user simulator contributes failures of its own; the probe's second kill clause measures that share). The failure time is not directly observed: the terminal step is a detection time, and the first unrecoverable step is located either by a judge (noisy; judge and verifier are different objects, the judge here is the locator and the database-state check is the verifier) or by counterfactual forking (the step after which resampled continuations succeed with probability below 0.1), which makes the observed data interval-censored failure times in the field's own terms; the estimand is the hazard over steps for the system under the stated protocol, and budget exhaustion is Type I censoring at T.

probe.design: tau-bench retail + airline (165 tasks) x 8 runs with one open-weight agent (e.g. Qwen3-32B class) and the standard GPT-class user simulator at tau-bench's default temperatures; log every turn and tool call. For each failed run record (a) the terminal turn, (b) the judge-located first unrecoverable turn (LLM judge with a 50-run human audit, agreement reported), (c) on 20 coin-flip tasks x 4 runs, counterfactual forks (4 continuations) every 3rd turn to locate the step where success probability drops below 0.1, as the gold standard against the judge. Mark budget-exhausted runs as right-censored. Fit per task a discrete-time Weibull (and a nonparametric Kaplan-Meier curve) to failure-step data; test gamma=1 by likelihood ratio against the constant-hazard (geometric) model; recompute pass^8 with censored runs excluded vs counted as failures. Second analysis: at each located failure step, resample only the user simulator's turn (4 draws) and record how often the outcome flips.
probe.cost: About 1,320 full episodes plus about 1,600 partial fork episodes: roughly $300-600 in API spend for the user simulator and judge plus about 60 GPU-hours (one 8xH100 node for a day) to serve the agent; 5 working days including the audit.
probe.kills_if: Dead if, across coin-flip tasks, the 95% interval for gamma contains 1 in 80% or more of tasks AND the likelihood-ratio test rejects the constant-hazard model in fewer than 20% of tasks: then the failure-step distribution carries no information beyond its mean and pass^k is sufficient. Reassigned to S1 (variance attribution), not an L1 reliability claim, if resampling only the user simulator's turn at the located failure step flips the outcome in more than 50% of cases: the hazard is then a property of the simulator. The censoring clause dies on its own if budget-exhausted runs are under 5% of failures for every model.

Choose the fix by hazard shape: a falling hazard (early-fork) says put RL credit and prompting effort on the first few turns; a rising hazard (wear-out) says schedule compaction or a restart at the hazard knee, the agent analogue of preventive replacement in reliability engineering (replace before the wear-out rise).

title: Per-task success as a drifting hidden state: observability and innovation tests for version change
abstract: In control theory and state estimation, reliability across versions is the problem of tracking a hidden state (each task's success probability in logit units) from noisy measurements (k binary run outcomes) and is solved by observability (the measurement structure fixes which functions of the hidden state are recoverable at all) plus the innovation test (compare each new measurement with the filter's prediction; the surprises are white with the predicted covariance when the model is right); carried into L1, that says a benchmark owner should treat each version's per-task results as innovations against a per-task tracker, and read a benchmark or harness change as a measurement-equation fault (innovations correlated across tasks that share the changed harness component, and flips of near-deterministic tasks) rather than as a state drift of the agent.

sentences: Observability: a hidden state can be recovered from the record of measurements if and only if the observability matrix (the stack C, CA, ..., CA^(n-1), where C is the measurement map and A the state transition) has full column rank; any state direction in its null space produces the same outputs as zero, and in the lecture notes' words 'no signal processing of any kind applied to u and y can deduce x' in that direction.

Innovation: the innovation is the measurement minus the filter's predicted measurement; when the filter's model and noise statistics are right, the normalized innovation sequence 'is a white Gaussian noise with zero mean and identity covariance matrix' (Mehra and Peschon 1971, as quoted by Hajiyev 2008), and with white measurement noise the innovations are white if and only if the process-noise model is right (IWAKF, arXiv 2604.21644).

Diagnostic: comparing the sample covariance or autocorrelation of the innovations with their predicted values detects a wrong model or a sensor fault online; which measurement channels' innovations move, and whether they stay correlated over time, is the evidence for which part of the model is wrong (Hajiyev tests the innovation covariance trace against identity for aircraft sensor faults).
sources: https://stanford.edu/class/ee363/lectures/observ.pdf — EE363 Lecture 5, 'Observability and state estimation' (Stanford, Winter 2008-09): observability matrix, rank condition, unobservable subspace, least-squares observer under noise

Hajiyev, 'Testing the Covariance Matrix of the Innovation Sequence in Application to Aircraft Sensor Fault Detection', IFAC World Congress 2008 (cites Mehra and Peschon 1971 for the white zero-mean identity-covariance property of normalized innovations)
https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.21644 — 'An Adaptive Kalman Filter that Learns the Coloring Dynamics of the Process Noise' (2026): innovations white iff process noise white, given white measurement noise

predicts.field_assumes: L1 today assumes the pinned control arm (re-run the old model on the new harness) is the separation device, and it is; and it already reads k runs through pass^k, which is exactly E_i[p_i^k], the k-th moment of the per-task success distribution — the full content of what k binary runs can observe about the task-level distribution.
predicts.would_change: An AUC above 0.9 would give closed-API benchmarks whose old versions are deprecated (no control arm possible) a who-moved detector from outcomes alone; that would add a column to HAL-style leaderboards. identifiability: Random given the task set, the harness version, the model version, and the sampling settings (temperature and seed) of the agent, of any simulated user and of any judge. From k runs of task i under version v, the recoverable functions of the hidden per-task state are exactly the moments E[p_i^j] for j <= k (binomial-mixture identifiability); with the standard k = 1 per task the per-task state is unobservable and only the task average is observable, and distinguishing 'coin-flip' tasks (p near 0.5) from 'bimodal' tasks (p near 0 or 1) needs k >= 2 (second moment 0.25 versus 0.5). At temperature 0 with a deterministic harness every p_i is 0 or 1 and the remaining run-to-run noise belongs to the harness, simulated user and judge, so the tracked quantity is a property of the protocol (agent + harness + judge), not of the agent alone. pass^k is this moment sequence under its lane name.
